description: We are the SPACESURVIVAL team, we want to participate in the challange which is in the game industry, we plan on to create a game that will educate and give the oppurtunity of expiriencing a real life space mission with a side of science-fiction. Our game is interactive and was made to give the player the best experience of an actual space mission.
summary:
Space Survival is a sci-fi survival game where players must survive a 30-day journey from Earth to Mars while managing limited resources and handling unexpected emergencies.

Inspired by 60 Seconds!, a game where you have to do major choices that effect you mental, health and hunger.

Our goal: Create an immersive space survival adventure where every decision matters.

Survive the journey. Reach Mars.
details:
Space Survival Project Details

How to Play Our Game

Space Survival is a browser-based, first-person survival game set aboard a spacecraft travelling to Mars. In a fictional scenario where environmental disasters threaten Earth, players must prepare for launch and survive a simulated 30-day journey. The game combines spacecraft exploration, resource management, and interactive operational tasks.

Figure 1. The illustrated mission prologue, depicting Earth’s environmental crisis, supply preparation, launch, and the journey to Mars.

Before launch, players choose up to 10 items from 27 available supplies. Each item displays its mass and purpose, allowing players to compare life-support equipment, engineering tools, medical supplies, and other survival resources. Limited cargo slots encourage players to establish priorities and consider which supplies will best support their mission.

Figure 2. The Cargo Bay selection screen, where players choose up to 10 survival supplies from 27 available items, each with a displayed mass and purpose.

After launch, players explore six locations: Crew Quarters, Main Corridor, Laboratory, Kitchen/Galley, Workout Room, and Control Room. They navigate using the on-screen room buttons or keyboard controls and interact with equipment inside each location.

Throughout the journey, players monitor health, food, hydration, energy, and psychological well-being. Activities require time and may consume resources while improving another aspect of survival. Players must therefore balance immediate needs with preventive maintenance and preparation for future problems.

Nine core technical and exercise minigames turn routine spacecraft responsibilities into interactive challenges. Each activity asks players to perform a specific procedure rather than simply select a maintenance command.

1. COLBERT Treadmill. Players alternate A and D footsteps while keeping their cadence within a green target zone. Completing the run awards fitness and health benefits, while its resource costs make exercise part of daily planning.

2. ARED Resistance Exercise. Players hold Space to lift the exercise bar, keep it inside the green target area, and release it below the reset line. The activity uses controlled lifting and release to represent resistance training in microgravity.

3. Earth Communications. Players adjust carrier frequency and dish alignment to match the Earth signal. After establishing a link, they choose predefined messages for a simulated Houston CAPCOM, such as telemetry reports or a family relay. The interface includes a simulated transmission delay.

Figure 3. The Earth communications minigame, showing signal alignment, carrier lock, and the simulated Deep Space Network link.

4. Power Bus Calibration. Players activate four electrical breakers in the displayed order, timing each activation to a green operating window. Mistimed actions produce arc faults and reduce the calibration rating.

5. Engine Core Containment. Players close three injector valves, vent pressure into the safe band, and time a magnetic containment lock. The sequence creates an escalating emergency in which an unresolved pressure problem can threaten the mission.

6. Navigation and Helm Control. Players steer through waypoint rings while avoiding debris, align the spacecraft with the target, and perform a simulated delta-v burn. A final trajectory adjustment completes the navigation sequence.

7. Airlock Seal Diagnostics. Players inspect four perimeter clamps, time their tightening actions to a green band, and equalize the pressure manifold. The task represents preventive maintenance intended to protect cabin pressure.

8. Microscope and Medicine Synthesis. Players adjust optical focus until the specimen is sharp, time a centrifuge action, and dispense a batch into the motion sickness medicine reserve. This is a fictional laboratory production mechanic rather than a real pharmaceutical procedure.

Figure 4. The laboratory microscope minigame, where players focus a specimen and time a centrifuge action to replenish the in-game medicine reserve.

9. Photobioreactor and Oxygen Replenishment. Players align three operating controls, charge an oxygen buffer, and inject the replenished oxygen into cabin life support. Pressure limits and energy costs add another trade-off to maintaining the spacecraft.

Figure 5. The oxygen replenishment minigame, showing the three operating controls used before charging the oxygen buffer.

Figure 6. The navigation minigame, where players steer through waypoint rings, avoid debris, and perform simulated delta-v burns to adjust the spacecraft’s trajectory.

The game also explores the human challenges of spaceflight. Players manage medical supplies and exercise using a treadmill and resistance equipment in the Workout Room. Exercise improves fitness and health while consuming resources, creating another decision about how to allocate the day’s time and supplies.

Figure 7. The spacecraft’s Workout Room, featuring a treadmill and resistance exercise equipment that players use to maintain fitness and health during transit.

In the Crew Quarters, players can view animal photographs as a recreational activity connected to the in-game sanity score. This introduces psychological well-being alongside the physical and technical demands of the mission.

Warnings identify approaching maintenance and medical deadlines, while a flight log records completed actions and important events. Missing a critical deadline can end the mission, even when other resources remain available. Players must pay attention to individual system warnings as well as their overall status indicators.

Figure 8. A game-over screen showing the consequence of missing an in-game medication deadline, alongside the mission’s final survival statistics.

The objective is to maintain both the astronaut and the spacecraft throughout the journey to Mars. Space Survival’s distinctive feature is the connection between equipment selection, spacecraft operations, and human needs. Its educational aim is to introduce competing priorities, resource planning, and the importance of preventive maintenance through interactive gameplay.

The fictional 30-day journey, percentage-based resources, medical deadlines, and simplified engineering procedures are gameplay abstractions rather than a validated mission simulation.

Boss Fights and Special Encounters

First Sleep Paralysis Encounter. During the transition from Day 5 to Day 6, the game introduces a fictional psychological boss encounter. Players use grounding-themed choices, including deep breathing, self-talk, and recalling a positive memory, between projectile-dodging phases. They move a small Mars-shaped avatar to avoid incoming stars and progress toward waking up.

Figure 9. The first sleep paralysis boss encounter, showing the grounding-themed choices available between action phases.

Figure 10. The projectile-dodging phase of the first boss encounter, where players steer the Mars-shaped avatar to avoid incoming stars.

Second Sleep Paralysis Encounter. During the transition from Day 24 to Day 25, the shadow returns with a different combat mechanic. Players watch its movement and press the matching direction using WASD or the arrow keys to counter attacks. Three waves shift the challenge from dodging to observation and reaction timing.

Day 18 Blackout Maze. A sudden power failure creates an exploration challenge rather than a direct combat encounter. Players guide a light through dark conduits, use sonar pulses to locate nearby breakers, and activate four circuits to restore spacecraft systems.

Emergency Antenna Repair. A separate repair sequence takes players to an exterior antenna interface. They clear three jammed gimbal clamps and adjust the dish’s azimuth and elevation to regain an Earth signal.

These encounters interrupt the routine of resource management with different kinds of pressure: reaction timing, directional counters, and navigation under limited visibility. The shadow encounters are fictional horror sequences, not literal external threats or validated medical simulations. The personal journal and wildlife photo archive provide quieter recreational activities between operational challenges.

Where and How We Used AI

We used both ChatGPT and Google AI Studio to assist with coding and creating some of the visual assets for Space Survival. These tools helped us translate our ideas into game features and develop visuals for the spacecraft setting.

Our team defined the game concept, mechanics, and visual direction, guiding the AI tools through our ideas and instructions. We made the decisions about which outputs to include and how they would fit into the game.

AI-generated visuals were used alongside separately sourced NASA animal photographs. These contributions have different origins: some visual assets were created with AI assistance, while the animal photographs were obtained from NASA.

Project source code and assets: space-survival.zip

The ZIP archive contains the game’s source code, configuration files, and visual and audio assets.

Where and How We Used NASA Resources

We consulted NASA educational materials and incorporated NASA animal photographs into Space Survival. These resources contributed scientific background and visual content to the project.

NASA’s Design and Develop Science Missions presentation provided background on mission planning, requirements, and the relationships between spacecraft systems and ground operations. It served as a conceptual reference for considering preparation, resource constraints, and operational decisions.

NASA Goddard’s How Solar Flares Affect Earth provided background on solar activity and its effects on Earth’s ionosphere. We consulted this material to explore space weather. Because the resource focuses on Earth’s atmosphere, we do not treat it as a direct model of astronaut radiation exposure during a Mars journey.

We also incorporated NASA wildlife photographs into an interactive archive in the Crew Quarters. Players can browse animal images and use the activity to improve their in-game sanity score. This connects NASA visual material with a recreational activity aboard the spacecraft; the numerical reward is a game mechanic.

Figure 11. The wildlife photo archive in the Crew Quarters, where players view NASA animal photographs as a recreational activity that improves the in-game sanity score.

The NASA materials served as educational and visual references. The project does not claim a live NASA data connection or NASA validation of the simulation. Numerical values, event schedules, and survival rules were simplified for gameplay.
